Foretold
for-tōld'
v. (told beforehand; of the Lord's warning to His disciples and of the prophets' united testimony to the days of Christ)
From fore- (before) and told. It renders Greek proereo in Mark 13:23, to say beforehand, and prokataggello in Acts 3:24, to announce in advance.

Biblical Definition

At the end of His warning about false christs and false prophets who would shew signs and wonders to seduce, the Lord says: “But take ye heed: behold, I have foretold you all things” (Mark 13:23). The forewarning is itself the protection — a disciple who has been told in advance is not to be surprised or swept away, and the command attached is take ye heed. Peter uses the word for the whole prophetic witness: “Yea, and all the prophets from Samuel and those that follow after, as many as have spoken, have likewise foretold of these days” (Acts 3:24). The claim is comprehensive — not that a few texts happen to fit, but that the entire line of prophets spoke of the days that had now arrived. He had said the same of the sufferings a few verses earlier: “those things, which God before had shewed by the mouth of all his prophets, that Christ should suffer, he hath so fulfilled” (Acts 3:18). Prophecy in the apostolic use is not primarily a puzzle to be decoded but a testimony already given, whose fulfilment vindicates both the Speaker and the Scriptures He spoke through.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines foretell as to predict, to tell before an event happens, and to foretoken or previously declare.

expand to see more

FORETELL, v.t. To predict; to tell before an event happens; to prophesy.

2. To foretoken; to foreshow.

FORETOLD, pp. Predicted; foreshown.

PROPHECY, n. A foretelling; prediction; a declaration of something to come.

FULFIL, v.t. To accomplish; to perform; to complete; to answer in event or by an event.

Key Scripture

Mark 13:23 — "But take ye heed: behold, I have foretold you all things."

Acts 3:24 — "Yea, and all the prophets from Samuel and those that follow after, as many as have spoken, have likewise foretold of these days."

Acts 3:18 — "But those things, which God before had shewed by the mouth of all his prophets, that Christ should suffer, he hath so fulfilled."

Deuteronomy 18:22 — "When a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken, but the prophet hath spoken it presumptuously: thou shalt not be afraid of him."

Modern Corruption

Prophecy is treated as a code for charting future events, and the New Testament treats it as testimony already given about Christ.

expand to see more

Peter says that all the prophets from Samuel onward foretold these days — the days of the crucified and risen Christ and the gospel going out from Jerusalem. That is how the apostles read the Old Testament, and it is a very different practice from the modern habit of mining the prophets for a timetable of events still future. Dispensational systems, unknown before the nineteenth century, have made prophecy chiefly a matter of charts and dates, and in doing so have quietly displaced its own stated subject. Whatever a reader concludes about the millennium — and Reformed orthodoxy has held more than one view — the prophets' announced theme, on apostolic authority, is Christ and His sufferings and the glory that should follow.

Mark 13:23 supplies the pastoral purpose of prediction, which is almost the opposite of curiosity. The Lord foretells deception, persecution and upheaval, and the application He draws is take ye heed. Foreknowledge of trouble is given so that believers will not be shaken by it when it comes, and specifically so that signs and wonders performed by false christs will not carry them away. A church absorbed in decoding current events has usually stopped doing the thing the passage actually commands, which is to watch, to hold fast, and to be unsurprised.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek proereo (G4280), to say beforehand — Mark 13:23, 2 Corinthians 13:2; prokataggello (G4293), to announce beforehand — Acts 3:24, 7:52; prophemi, the root of prophecy.

expand to see more

Greek proereo (G4280) — to speak before; Mark 13:23, and Galatians 1:9 of what Paul had said already.

Greek prokataggello (G4293) — to announce beforehand; Acts 3:24, and Acts 7:52 of the prophets who shewed before of the coming of the Just One.

Greek propascho and pathema — the sufferings foretold; Acts 3:18, that Christ should suffer.

Greek blepo (G991) — to look, take heed; Mark 13:23, the command attached to the foretelling.

1 Peter 1:11 states the prophets' own subject: the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow.

Usage

"“Behold, I have foretold you all things” — and the command is take ye heed."

"“All the prophets from Samuel… have likewise foretold of these days”."

"Prophecy's announced subject is Christ, on apostolic authority."
